newsitem.title: UK: IPE Brent soften on Iraq, IEA forecasts.
newsitem.headline: IPE Brent soften on Iraq, IEA forecasts.

text.p: IPE Brent crude oil futures were slightly weaker on Tuesday after Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the U.N. appeared a step closer to getting back on track, traders said.

August Brent crude oil was two cents a barrel weaker at 0939 GMT and stood at $18.17, while July gas oil was $1.50 firmer at $162.75. Gas oil's rise was seen as a catch-up to late gains in Brent on Monday.
"It is the Iraqi announcement more than anything else," one IPE dealer said.
The U.N. coordinator in Baghdad said on Tuesday he hoped the world body would receive Iraq's food distribution plan by 2000 GMT.
The six-month $2 billion oil-for-food plan was renewed a month ago but Iraq's oil exports have been delayed, pending completion of the government's distribution and procurement plans.
Traders also said they thought bearish predictions from the International Energy Agency (IEA) had exerted a little bearish influence.
The IEA said oil prices would fall further this year as stocks rise, despite higher-than-expected gasoline demand in the U.S.

While the organisation revised upwards its estimates for world oil demand in 1997 and 1998 by 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 73.8 million and 75.6 million, it added: "Projections of world demand and non-OPEC supply for the remainder of the year suggest that there will be very substantial increases in inventories, unless OPEC crude oil output is reduced significantly."

"The return of Iraqi crude to the export markets is the most important near-term wild card for world oil supply," the IEA said. "Over the last two weeks opinions regarding the likely date have varied widely, ranging from mid-July to mid-August."
Oil traders were also awaiting weekly U.S. oil industry data, which was expected to emerge on time on Tuesday night despite the Fourth of July holiday in the U.S.
Both the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Department of Energy (DoE) said their data would be issued as usual after the market's close on Tuesday.
